name: Benamara 2020 GEP explicit WAT model (density, wax, pour point, freezing point)
equation_text: WAT = [11.14 x Wt^6 x (Wt/d - 6.329)]/(2.815 Wt + 1.407 FP) + 12.15A + 12.24B + C + D + E, with A = 5th root(d - PP + 22.1317 Wt - 14.4856 Wt^2 + (PP - FP) Wt); B = [7.0155 Wt^3 + FP - exp(Wt) - tanh(Wt)] inside an unreadable function; C = -884.7 tanh[Wt^2 - exp(d - Wt)] + 4053; D = -0.09917 exp(exp(-Wt)/log(Wt)) + 869.1 exp(-(0.249 exp(Wt)) / (d ... 2.482 exp(Wt))); E = -(0.0482(d + FP) - 1.146)/(230.6 Wt^2 - 1371) - 1359.397 (PP - Wt + FP + 23.72031)/FP. GROUPING RECONSTRUCTED FROM A GARBLED TEXT EXTRACTION.
python:
def wat_gep_literal(d, Wt, PP, FP):
    import numpy as np
    r5 = lambda x: np.sign(x)*abs(x)**0.2
    T1 = 11.14*Wt**6*(Wt/d - 6.329)/(2.815*Wt + 1.407*FP)
    A = r5(d - PP + 22.1317*Wt - 14.4856*Wt**2 + (PP - FP)*Wt)
    B = np.tanh(7.0155*Wt**3 + FP - np.exp(Wt) - np.tanh(Wt))
    C = -884.7*np.tanh(Wt**2 - np.exp(d - Wt)) + 4053
    D = -0.09917*np.exp(np.exp(-Wt)/np.log(Wt)) + 869.1*np.exp(-0.249*np.exp(Wt)/d - 2.482*np.exp(Wt))
    E = -(0.0482*(d + FP) - 1.146)/(230.6*Wt**2 - 1371) - 1359.397*(PP - Wt + FP + 23.72031)/FP
    return T1 + 12.15*A + 12.24*B + C + D + E
fitted_on: 59 Algerian crude oils (data in master_v9 as algeria_benamara_01..59); WAT by rotational pour point tester
reported_accuracy: GEP overall R2 0.9143, AARD 0.5484 pct, RMSE 2.1757 K; training R2 0.9597; testing R2 0.7203, AARD 1.1977 pct, RMSE 4.3977 K (Table 3)
citation: Benamara, C., Gharbi, K., Nait Amar, M., Hamada, B. (2020). Prediction of Wax Appearance Temperature Using Artificial Intelligent Techniques. Arabian Journal for Science and Engineering, 45, 1319-1330.
notes: NOT REPRODUCIBLE from the text copy. Our literal reading (tanh for B, natural log, the D second term as written) reproduces Table 4 row 1 (d 0.812, Wt 2.44, PP 264.15, FP 262.55, WAT 278.85 K) to within 0.3 K, but misses rows 2 to 5 by 150 to 3000 K, so at least the C term, the Wt^6 term and B are misread. About 1000 alternative groupings were tried; none fits all 5 rows. Needs the Springer PDF. Also it needs freezing point, which few crude datasets report. Do not use for generation.

name: Cloud point blending rule (power law, exponent 13.45)
equation_text: CP_b^13.45 = sum_i V_i CP_i^13.45, CP in Rankine
python:
def cp_blend(V, CP):
    import numpy as np
    R = (np.asarray(CP, float) + 273.15)*1.8
    return (np.sum(np.asarray(V, float)*R**13.45))**(1/13.45)/1.8 - 273.15
fitted_on: diesel blends (Semwal and Varshney, data not seen)
citation: Semwal, P.B., Varshney, R.G. (1995). Predictions of pour, cloud and cold filter plugging point for future diesel fuels with application to diesel blending models. Fuel, 74(3), 437-444. Read via ECNet software documentation (ecnet.blends.cloud_point).
notes: Useful for making synthetic blends of two real crudes or cuts: the blend is pulled toward the waxier component more than a linear average. 50/50 blend of -10 C and +10 C gives +2.2 C. Applied to the Penn State pour point example (0.687 at -6 F, 0.313 at 40 F) it gives 14.9 F against 15 F from the PPBI chart (exponent 12.5 gives 14.4 F), so the same power law also works for pour point blending. Hu-Burns form is the same with exponent 1/x, x 0.05 originally, updated to 0.073 to 0.186 depending on range for pour point (Semwal and Varshney 1994 OGJ). Probable DOI 10.1016/0016-2361(95)93479-Z (from memory, not confirmed).

def pp_blend(V, PP, x=0.079):

fitted_on: 64 fuel oil blends, pour point by ASTM D97 (Semwal and Varshney update)
reported_accuracy: new 2-parameter forms 5 to 30 pct more accurate than updated Hu-Burns
citation: Semwal, P.B., Varshney, R.G. (1994). New pour point correlations improve economics of distillate blending. Oil and Gas Journal, June 6, 1994 (updated x values); form from Hu, J., Burns, A.M. (1970). Index predicts cloud, pour and flash points of distillate fuel blends. Hydrocarbon Processing, 49(11), 213-216.
where: text (x values and ranges); power-law form as in ECNet cloud point rule
notes: The OGJ web text gives the x values and ranges but not the printed equation; the power-law form is the standard Hu-Burns index and matches the ECNet cloud point rule (1/0.0743 = 13.45). Check against Penn State chart example (0.687 at -6 F and 0.313 at 40 F): x 0.079 gives 14.5 F (-9.72 C) vs 15 F from the PPBI chart.

name: Coutinho et al. 2006 melting temperature of n-paraffins (used above C40)
notes: N 20 gives 309.5 K (n-C20 measured about 309.6 K); N 40 gives 354.9 K (n-C40 about 354.6 K). Tends to 421.6 K for very long chains (polyethylene limit), so it is the physically safe choice for heavy wax tails; Won's form keeps rising without limit.
citation: Coutinho, J.A.P., Edmonds, B., Moorwood, T., Szczepanski, R., Zhang, X. (2006). Reliable wax predictions for flow assurance. Energy and Fuels, 20(3), 1081-1088.

name: Coutinho et al. 2006 enthalpy of fusion of n-paraffins (total, linear)
notes: N 20 gives 62.9 kJ/mol. About 3.8 kJ/mol per CH2 group.
citation: Coutinho, J.A.P., Edmonds, B., Moorwood, T., Szczepanski, R., Zhang, X. (2006). Reliable wax predictions for flow assurance. Energy and Fuels, 20(3), 1081-1088.

name: Coutinho et al. 2006 enthalpy of fusion from rotator phase, C8-C40
notes: N 20 gives 46.5 kJ/mol, lower than the total enthalpy of Eq. 3 because the solid-solid (rotator) part is excluded.
citation: Coutinho, J.A.P., Edmonds, B., Moorwood, T., Szczepanski, R., Zhang, X. (2006). Reliable wax predictions for flow assurance. Energy and Fuels, 20(3), 1081-1088.

name: Coutinho et al. 2006 rotator to orthorhombic transition temperature
notes: N 25 gives 319.6 K (n-C25 transition measured about 320 K).
citation: Coutinho, J.A.P., Edmonds, B., Moorwood, T., Szczepanski, R., Zhang, X. (2006). Reliable wax predictions for flow assurance. Energy and Fuels, 20(3), 1081-1088.
